changes.after: Apply can work across the rows or down the columns of a matrix.

before: apply(m, 1, sum) applies sum to each row; margin 2 selects columns. Matrix filling is column-major by default, so these rows contain 1,3,5 and 2,4,6.

apply operates on arrays and may convert a data frame to a matrix first. Mixing character and numeric columns can therefore coerce all cells to text. For plain numeric totals, rowSums or colSums are more direct; apply is not automatically faster than every explicit alternative.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
cat(apply(m, 1, sum), "\n")
```
Expected output or behavior: 9 12. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Compare apply(m, 1, sum) with rowSums(m) on this numeric matrix. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Apply can work across the rows or down the columns of a matrix.
The one here chooses rows. A two in the same spot would choose columns.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```r
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
cat(apply(m, 1, sum), "\n")
```
The output is `9 12`. The first row adds to nine and the second adds to twelve.
